extracted.intended_audience: geographers, natural philosophers, and educated readers of physical geography
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and principles for studying and interpreting the form, elevation, and distribution of continents and seas, and their influence on climate, vegetation, and human society using comparative, numerical, and stratigraphic evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority: quantity of land raised and individual configuration
rubrics_metrics.description: Among the general subjects of contemplation appertaining to a work of this nature, a prominent place must be given, first, in the consideration of the 'quantity' of the land raised above the level of the sea, and next, to the individual configuration of each part, either in relation to horizontal extension (relations of form) or to vertical elevation (hypsometrical relations of mountain-chains).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When studying continents, put first the amount of emerged land, then study each region's shape (horizontal relations of form) and height (hypsometry). Both axes (horizontal and vertical) are essential dimensions of analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for reciprocal action of air, sea, and land
rubrics_metrics.description: A knowledge of the reciprocal action of air, sea, and land teaches us that great meteorological phenomena can not be comprehended when considered independently of geognostic relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Climate (the character of the atmosphere) depends on oceanic currents of differing temperatures and radiation from land, which varies with form, elevation, color, and vegetation; therefore meteorology must be integrated with geognostic (geological/geographical) study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use accurate numerical observations of the sea (temperature, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is only during the subsequent period that numerous accurate observations on the temperature of the sea at different latitudes and at different seasons have been made and numerically compared together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Progress in meteorology and climatic inference requires systematic, quantitative sea-temperature measurements across latitudes and seasons and numerical comparison between them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure and consider ratios of solid to fluid surface
rubrics_metrics.description: In the present condition of the surface of our planet, the area of the solid is to that of the fluid parts as 1:2 4/5ths (according to Rigaud, as 100:270).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate and use the proportion of land to sea (and islands as a fraction of continental mass) because this relation strongly influences temperature distribution, atmospheric pressure variations, wind directions, and moisture availability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative configuration analysis (coastline/mirror analogies)
rubrics_metrics.description: In this Atlantic valley, as is almost every where the case in the configuration of large continental masses, coasts deeply indented, and rich in islands, are situated opposite to those possessing a different character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare opposite coasts and continental outlines (e.g., western Africa vs. South America, parallels of indentation) to identify repeated analogies and infer geognostic relations; use such comparisons cautiously as suggestive evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use stratigraphic relationships to assign relative ages to mountain systems
rubrics_metrics.description: According to the grand views of Elie de Beaumont, we must ascribe a relative age to each system of mountain chains on the supposition that their elevation must necessarily have occurred between the period of the deposition of the vertically elevated strata and that of the horizontally inclined strata running at the base of the mountains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine relative ages of uplifts by observing the sequence of strata (vertically elevated versus horizontally inclined at the base); stratigraphic position provides a criterion for dating or ordering mountain-building events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat subterranean forces as primary causes of continental elevation
rubrics_metrics.description: All that we know regarding this subject resolves itself into this one point, that the active cause is subterranean; that continents did not arise at once in the form they now present, but were... increased by degrees by means of numerous oscillatory elevations and depressions of the soil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret large-scale elevations and the formation of continents primarily in terms of internal (subterranean) forces and oscillatory movements of the crust, supported by analogy to volcanic phenomena and observed geological features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the dual causation: internal (accidental direction) and surface forces
rubrics_metrics.description: Their present form is, therefore, the result of two causes... the first is the expression of subterranean force, whose direction we term accidental... while the second is derived from forces acting on the surface, among which volcanic eruptions, the elevation of mountains, and currents of sea water play the principal parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for both internal tectonic drivers (whose directions may appear 'accidental') and external surface processes (volcanism, sea currents, erosion, deposition) when explaining continental form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantify mountain mass/volume to assess impact on continental elevation
rubrics_metrics.description: Since grand and lofty mountain chains so strongly excite our imagination... it is the more necessary to demonstrate, by a correct numerical estimation of their volume, how small is the quantity of their elevated mass when compared with the area of the adjacent continents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform numerical estimations of mountain volumes and compute their potential effect on mean continental elevation (examples: Pyrenees would raise France ~115 feet; Alps ~21.5 feet for Europe) to avoid misleading impressions from visual prominence alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mark and record ancient sea-levels (benchmarks) for epochal comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: I urged the necessity of causing marks to be cut in the rocks of the southern hemisphere, as had already been done in Sweden and on the shores of the Caspian Sea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish physical marks (benchmarks) indicating mean sea level at known epochs in different localities to detect secular changes in relative land/sea levels and to enable spatial comparisons of simultaneous elevation/depression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on barometer alone to infer general sea-level change
rubrics_metrics.description: But as the mean pressure of the atmosphere at the level of the sea is not the same at all latitudes, owing to meteorological causes... the barometer alone can not afford a certain evidence of the general change of level in the ocean.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat barometric readings with caution for inferring sea-level trends because atmospheric pressure varies by latitude, season, and meteorological conditions; corroborate with other measures (trigonometry, benchmarks, tide records).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish gradual secular movements from earthquake-induced changes
rubrics_metrics.description: This latter phenomenon, which is well attested by historical evidence, must not be confounded with the changes in the level of the soil occasioned by earthquakes, as on the shores of Chili and of Cutch...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate slow, region-wide secular uplift/subsidence (e.g., Swedish uplift) from sudden, localized vertical displacements due to earthquakes; analyze spatial patterns and historical/trigonometrical records to separate causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt long-timescale perspective: small rates accumulate to large changes
rubrics_metrics.description: The eastern coast of the Scandinavian peninsula has probably risen about 320 feet in the space of 8000 years... What are such intervals of time compared to the length of the geognostic periods revealed to us in the stratified series of formations?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret observed small secular rates (feet per century/millennium) in the context of geological timescales; appreciate that incremental movements accumulate to major landscape changes over geognostic periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid treating analogies as fixed laws of form
rubrics_metrics.description: We have collected facts and brought forward some analogies of configuration in distant parts of the earth, but we do not venture to regard them as fixed laws of form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use analogies and repeated configurations as heuristic or suggestive, but avoid asserting universal deterministic laws from such analogies without further evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze littoral and internal articulation for climatic, economic, and social effects
rubrics_metrics.description: As the 'external' configuration of continents... exercises, by their variously indented littoral outlines, a favorable influence on climate, trade, and the progress of civilization, so likewise does their internal articulation, or the vertical elevation of the soil... give rise to equally important results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing regions, consider how coastal articulation (bays, islands, indentations) and internal relief (mountains, plateaux, valleys) affect climatic processes, navigation/trade accessibility, agricultural diversity, and the social/intellectual development of populations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple lines of empirical evidence (fossils, shell-banks, trigonometrical surveys)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lines marking the ancient level of the sea in pre-historic times are indicated... by banks of shells identical with those of the present seas... The depression of the Dead Sea has been successively determined by the barometrical measurements... and by the trigonometrical survey of Lieutenant Symond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine paleontological (fossil remains), geomorphological (shell-banks), geodetic (trigonometrical surveys), and careful instrumented measures to reconstruct past sea levels and land elevations and to validate interpretations.
